title: Fantasy Map Quest — Part 1: Grid Coordinates & Realm Cartography
topic: Reference Frames, Grid Coordinate Systems, and Map Scales
summary: Launch the 3-day Fantasy Map Quest: student partners establish reference frames, coordinate grid origins (0,0), compass roses, map scale factors, and sketch fantasy geography.
activity: Fantasy Map Quest (Day 1 of 3): In 45-minute periods (~30 min work time), student pairs establish a home village origin point (0,0), draw a four-direction compass rose, define a map scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 leagues), and sketch terrain featuring 4 required quest landmarks (Village -> Forest/Swamp -> Mountain Pass -> Citadel).
essentialQuestion: How does our choice of reference point determine whether an object is considered in motion or at rest?

wicor.Writing: Documenting landmark coordinate points (x, y) and recording the map scale conversion rule.
wicor.Inquiry: Investigating how changing the map origin shifts all landmark coordinates without altering land geography.
wicor.Collaboration: Partner cartography teams dividing duties: grid calibration, terrain sketching, and landmark naming.
wicor.Organization: Setting up the 3-day project quest log, data tables, and scale keys.
wicor.Reading: Interpreting compass rose bearings and coordinate grid legends.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: You discover an ancient map that says: 'Walk 50 paces to find the buried treasure.' Why is this instruction completely useless on its own? What two specific pieces of information do you need before you can take a single step?
bellRinger.explanation: You need to know: (1) Where to start (the Reference Point / Origin), and (2) Which direction to walk (Direction / Compass Heading). Without an origin and direction, 50 paces could be anywhere in a 360-degree circle.

title: Fantasy Map Quest — Part 2: Winding Trails & Distance vs. Displacement
topic: Curved Path Length (String Technique) vs. Straight-Line Vector Displacement
summary: Day 2 of the quest project: students plot a meandering adventurer route, measure curved path lengths with string (total distance), and draw direct vector arrows from origin (displacement).
activity: Fantasy Map Quest (Day 2 of 3): Partners draw the traveler's winding trail connecting all 4 landmarks. Using string pressed along the curves, students measure paper centimeters for Legs 1, 2, and 3, convert to realm units, and calculate total distance traveled. They then draw a direct straight-line vector arrow from the Origin to Destination, measuring net displacement magnitude and compass direction.
essentialQuestion: Why is the total distance traveled by an adventurer almost always greater than their net displacement?

wicor.Writing: Writing clear definitions of scalar distance and vector displacement based on empirical trail measurements.
wicor.Inquiry: Discovering why winding around obstacles inflates distance while leaving displacement unchanged.
wicor.Collaboration: One partner lays and pinches the measurement string while the other records ruler readings and computes scale conversions.
wicor.Organization: Recording multi-leg measurement data in a four-column table (Leg, Paper cm, Scale Factor, Realm Units).
wicor.Reading: Tracing complex path geometries and measuring directional angles.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: An adventurer leaves their home village, travels 15 miles north to an ancient temple, and then travels 15 miles south back to their village. What is their total distance traveled, and what is their net displacement?
bellRinger.explanation: Total distance traveled is 30 miles (15 + 15), but net displacement is 0 miles because their final position is identical to their starting position (Δx = x_final - x_initial = 0).

title: Fantasy Map Quest — Part 3: Travel Time, Speed & The Homecoming Paradox
topic: Calculating Average Speed (v = d / t), Round-Trip Vectors & Peer Audit
summary: Conclude the 3-day project: students add travel time across terrain hazards, calculate speed per leg (v = d/t), resolve the round-trip return paradox, and complete peer audits.
activity: Fantasy Map Quest (Day 3 of 3): Teams assign travel durations (days/hours) to each leg based on terrain difficulty (swamps take longer than plains!) and calculate average speeds (v = d / t). Teams solve the 'Homecoming Paradox' (traveler returns home: distance doubles, displacement = 0), complete the analysis questions, and swap maps with another team for peer verification.
essentialQuestion: How can a traveler embark on a long, arduous journey covering immense distance, yet end up with an average velocity of zero?

wicor.Writing: Writing narrative quest summaries and scientific justifications for the Homecoming Paradox.
wicor.Inquiry: Testing how terrain difficulty alters travel time and average speed across identical distances.
wicor.Collaboration: Swapping completed maps with a partner team to audit calculations and verify vector measurements.
wicor.Organization: Synthesizing all calculations, graphs, and written conclusions into the final project submission.
wicor.Reading: Reading and auditing peer map legends, quest logs, and scale calculations.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If a traveler walks 40 leagues through an enchanted forest over 8 days, what is the traveler's average speed in leagues per day?
bellRinger.explanation: Average speed is v = d / t = 40 leagues / 8 days = 5 leagues per day.

title: "The Monster's Journey" Constant Velocity Lab
topic: Multi-Interval Kinematic Data Collection (Tumble Buggy Lab)
summary: Empirical inquiry using motorized constant-speed tumble buggies to record position stamps every 2 seconds and verify uniform motion.
activity: Students release battery-operated motorized cars down meter tracks, drop beanbag markers every 2 seconds on audible cues, measure cumulative positions, record coordinate pairs in tables, and test whether displacement increments remain constant across time intervals.
essentialQuestion: How can multi-stage empirical data reveal whether an object travels with truly uniform motion?

wicor.Writing: Writing a formal experimental conclusion explaining whether the buggy maintained true constant speed.
wicor.Inquiry: Analyzing experimental variances in beanbag placement to identify measurement error vs genuine motor slowing.
wicor.Collaboration: Coordinating stopwatch calls and physical marker drops in synchronized rhythm.
wicor.Organization: Constructing clean position-time data tables ready for graphing.
wicor.Reading: Following multi-step laboratory protocols and safety guidelines.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If a toy car moves at a steady, constant speed of 0.5 meters per second, how far will it travel in 6 seconds?
bellRinger.explanation: Using d = v · t: distance = 0.5 m/s · 6 s = 3.0 meters.

title: Graphing Motion: Position vs. Time (x-t) Slopes
topic: Coordinate Graphing & Slope Interpretation (m = Δx / Δt)
summary: Translate tumble buggy lab data into position vs. time graphs and prove that coordinate slope directly equals physical speed.
activity: Interactive Graphing Workshop: Students use graph paper and the digital Distance vs Time App to plot position-time data, draw best-fit trendlines, calculate coordinate slope (m = Δy / Δx = Δx / Δt), compare steep lines (fast) vs shallow lines (slow), and decode horizontal lines (at rest).
essentialQuestion: How does the geometric slope of a position-time graph directly encode physical speed?

wicor.Writing: Writing narrative explanations describing the physical journey represented by each line segment.
wicor.Inquiry: Investigating how line steepness changes when an object speeds up or slows down.
wicor.Collaboration: Peer-checking coordinate slope calculations (rise over run).
wicor.Organization: Properly labeling graph axes with variable names, symbols, and metric units [Position (m) vs Time (s)].
wicor.Reading: Decoding graphic representations of multi-segment journeys.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: On a position-time graph, what does a completely flat, horizontal line indicate about the object's motion?
bellRinger.explanation: A flat, horizontal line means position is not changing over time (Δx = 0), so velocity is zero—the object is stationary (at rest).

title: Labor Day — No School
topic: Labor Day Holiday (No School)
summary: Labor Day Holiday observed. No school scheduled.
activity: No school in observance of the Labor Day holiday.
essentialQuestion: Holiday observed — no school.

title: Decoding Acceleration: When Velocity Changes
topic: Definition of Acceleration (a = Δv / Δt) & Metric Units (m/s²)
summary: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, break down the units of m/s², and analyze the three distinct physical ways to accelerate.
activity: Three Ways to Accelerate Video Telemetry Sprint: Students analyze automotive telemetry clips (gas pedal = speeding up, brake pedal = slowing down, steering wheel = changing direction). Students calculate acceleration rates from changing velocity readings over time.
essentialQuestion: Why is a vehicle turning a corner at constant speed still considered accelerating in physics?

wicor.Writing: Defining why m/s² represents '(meters per second) gained every second'.
wicor.Inquiry: Dissecting real-world car test track data to calculate braking vs launching acceleration rates.
wicor.Collaboration: Partner problem-solving calculating positive and negative acceleration.
wicor.Organization: Constructing formula breakdown cards: a = (v_final - v_initial) / Δt.
wicor.Reading: Reading technical automobile specifications (e.g. 0 to 60 mph times) and converting to SI units.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: A car sitting at a red light steps on the gas and reaches 20 m/s in 4.0 seconds. What is the car's average acceleration?
bellRinger.explanation: Acceleration is a = (v_final - v_initial) / t = (20 m/s - 0 m/s) / 4.0 s = 5.0 m/s².

title: Velocity vs. Time (v-t) Graphs: Slope & Area
topic: Graphing Acceleration & Area Under the Curve (Area = Δx)
summary: Connect constant velocity (flat v-t line) with uniform acceleration (sloped v-t line), and discover that the area under a v-t graph yields displacement.
activity: Graph Matching & Area Challenge: Students work in pairs to match position-time curves with corresponding velocity-time graphs. Teams compute the geometric area (rectangles and triangles) beneath v-t line segments to determine total displacement.
essentialQuestion: How can the geometric area under a velocity-time graph reveal the total distance an object moved?

wicor.Writing: Writing step-by-step mathematical proofs showing how geometric area calculates displacement.
wicor.Inquiry: Deducing why the slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration.
wicor.Collaboration: Pair-matching dual graph sets and reconciling disagreements on curve shapes.
wicor.Organization: Color-coding graph features: blue for slope (acceleration), green for area (displacement).
wicor.Reading: Translating multi-part velocity graphs into verbal motion stories.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If an object travels at a constant velocity of 6 m/s for 5 seconds, what is the geometric shape of its velocity-time graph, and what is its displacement?
bellRinger.explanation: The v-t graph is a horizontal line at 6 m/s forming a rectangle with height 6 and base 5. The area is 6 m/s · 5 s = 30 meters displacement.

title: "Marble Race" Ramp Incline Lab
topic: Quantitative Incline Acceleration Investigation
summary: Inquiry lab investigating how ramp elevation angle affects the acceleration and final velocity of rolling spheres down tracks.
activity: Students set up grooved incline ramps at 5°, 10°, and 15° angles. Using stopwatch intervals or photogate checkpoints, students record split times at multiple distances, plot velocity vs time, calculate acceleration slopes, and determine how ramp steepness governs acceleration.
essentialQuestion: How does ramp inclination quantitatively govern the rate of acceleration down an incline?

wicor.Writing: Writing an evidence-based lab report summarizing the correlation between ramp angle and acceleration.
wicor.Inquiry: Formulating hypotheses on how doubling track angle impacts final rollout velocity.
wicor.Collaboration: Dividing duties: angle surveyor, release coordinator, gate timer, and data logger.
wicor.Organization: Plotting multi-angle trials on a single coordinate graph to visually compare slope steepness.
wicor.Reading: Reading angle protractors and photogate sensor instructions accurately.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: When a marble rolls down a frictionless ramp, does its speed remain constant, or does it accelerate? How do you know?
bellRinger.explanation: It accelerates. A component of gravity pulls it forward continuously down the incline, causing it to cover greater distances in each subsequent second.

title: Free Fall & Earth's Gravitational Acceleration
topic: Free Fall Kinematics & Air Resistance Boundaries (g = 9.8 m/s²)
summary: Investigate free fall near Earth's surface, explore Galileo's insight that mass does not change fall rate in a vacuum, and analyze air drag terminal velocity.
activity: Drop-Sensor Inquiry & Apollo Moon Video Analysis: Students drop solid steel marbles vs light plastic spheres from 1.0m and 2.0m heights to measure drop times. Students analyze Apollo 15 footage of the hammer and feather dropped on the Moon to prove gravitational equivalence.
essentialQuestion: Why do heavy and light objects fall at identical rates in the absence of air resistance?

wicor.Writing: Explaining why air resistance causes a flat paper to fall slower than a crumpled ball of identical mass.
wicor.Inquiry: Evaluating why our daily experience fools us into thinking heavy objects fall faster.
wicor.Collaboration: Working in teams to film slow-motion drop tests and calculate empirical g values.
wicor.Organization: Tabulating freefall drop distances using the formula Δy = ½ · g · t².
wicor.Reading: Analyzing historical accounts of Galileo's inclined plane and tower thought experiments.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If you drop an elephant and a golf ball at the exact same instant from a tall cliff on the Moon (where there is no air), which lands first?
bellRinger.explanation: They land at the exact same time! In the absence of air resistance, all objects accelerate at the exact same rate regardless of mass.

title: The Big Question: What Keeps Things Moving? (Inertia Demos)
topic: Inquiry Launch into Dynamics: Aristotle vs Galileo vs Newton
summary: Launch Dynamics with high-engagement inertia demonstrations that dismantle the intuitive misconception that motion requires a continuous forward push.
activity: Inertia Phenomenon Stations: Students cycle through 4 hands-on stations: (1) The Tablecloth Pull with weighted dishes, (2) The Index Card & Penny snap into a beaker, (3) The Bowling Ball Mallet Challenge (steering a rolling ball), and (4) The Frictionless Hover Puck gliding indefinitely across the floor.
essentialQuestion: Does an object in motion require a continuous applied force to keep moving forward?

wicor.Writing: Writing initial claim statements answering what happens to an object when all friction is removed.
wicor.Inquiry: Observing how objects resist changes to their current state of rest or motion.
wicor.Collaboration: Group rotation through demonstration stations, debating observations.
wicor.Organization: Completing a four-quadrant observation sheet detailing cause, observation, and inference for each demo.
wicor.Reading: Reading excerpts from Aristotle's motion theories vs Galileo's thought experiments.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If you throw a baseball in deep outer space where there is no gravity, no air, and no friction, what will happen to the ball after it leaves your hand?
bellRinger.explanation: The baseball will keep moving in a straight line at the exact same constant speed forever, because there is no net force to slow it down or change its direction.

title: Newton's First Law of Motion (The Law of Inertia)
topic: The First Law & Natural States of Motion
summary: Formalize Newton's First Law: objects maintain constant velocity (rest or steady straight-line motion) unless acted upon by a net external force.
activity: AVID Critical Reading & CER Writing: Students read Galileo's double-incline thought experiment. Teams draft Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) paragraphs analyzing why unrestrained vehicle passengers lurch forward during emergency braking.
essentialQuestion: How does Newton's First Law redefine our everyday definition of what forces actually do?

wicor.Writing: Drafting formal CER arguments justifying passenger motion during sudden vehicle turns.
wicor.Inquiry: Exploring why our intuition makes us feel an imaginary 'push' when a vehicle accelerates.
wicor.Collaboration: Peer-editing CER evidence statements with structured partner rubrics.
wicor.Organization: Highlighting text claims and evidence using color-coded AVID markup strategies.
wicor.Reading: Annotating scientific text on Newton's First Law and inertial reference frames.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: When a car takes a sharp left turn, why do passengers feel like they are being thrown to the right?
bellRinger.explanation: No force pushes passengers right. Due to inertia, their bodies naturally continue moving straight ahead until the car door or seatbelt exerts an unbalanced force pushing them left into the turn.

title: Mass as the Quantitative Measure of Inertia
topic: Mass (kg) vs. Weight (N) vs. Volume: Isolating Inertia
summary: Establish mass as the measure of an object's inertia, fundamentally distinguishing it from gravitational weight (N) and geometric volume.
activity: Mystery Mass Inertia Shaker Lab: Blindfolded students shake identical sealed cylinders filled with cotton, wood, and lead horizontally along low-friction tracks. Because vertical gravity is supported, students rank cylinder masses purely through tactile resistance to back-and-forth acceleration.
essentialQuestion: Why would an anvil have the exact same inertia in deep space as it does on Earth, even though it weighs zero Newtons?

wicor.Writing: Explaining the physical difference between an object's mass in kilograms and weight in Newtons.
wicor.Inquiry: Testing whether shaking objects horizontally isolates mass from gravitational weight.
wicor.Collaboration: Comparing blind shaker rankings across lab table teams to reach consensus.
wicor.Organization: Constructing a three-way distinction matrix: Mass, Weight, and Volume.
wicor.Reading: Reading technical scales and spring force indicators with appropriate units.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: Which has greater inertia: a 10 kg bowling ball on Earth or a 10 kg bowling ball floating on the International Space Station?
bellRinger.explanation: They have the exact same inertia! Inertia depends solely on mass (10 kg), which does not change based on gravitational location.

title: The Force Toolkit: Types of Forces & Free-Body Diagrams
topic: Contact vs. Field Forces & Systematic Free-Body Modeling (FBDs)
summary: Catalog standard physical forces (Gravity, Normal, Tension, Friction, Applied) and master drawing standardized Free-Body Diagrams (FBDs).
activity: Whiteboard FBD Drafting Sprint: Students rotate through physical stations (book resting on desk, sled pulled across snow, elevator accelerating upward, hanging traffic light) and draw isolated dot diagrams with correctly labeled and scaled vector arrows.
essentialQuestion: How do free-body diagrams allow us to translate messy real-world objects into isolated vector systems?

wicor.Writing: Labeling force vectors with standard subscript notations: F_g, F_N, F_f, F_T, F_app.
wicor.Inquiry: Identifying which surfaces exert contact forces versus non-contact gravitational field forces.
wicor.Collaboration: Pair critique of whiteboard diagrams: verifying equal vector lengths for balanced situations.
wicor.Organization: Creating an FBD reference cheat sheet mapping scenarios to force combinations.
wicor.Reading: Extracting physical force interactions from descriptive word problems.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: A textbook sits motionless on a classroom table. What two forces act on the book, and how do their magnitudes compare?
bellRinger.explanation: Gravity (F_g) pulls downward and the Normal force (F_N) of the table pushes upward. They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

title: Balanced Forces & Mechanical Equilibrium (F_net = 0)
topic: Static and Dynamic Equilibrium: Zero Net Force implies Zero Acceleration
summary: Compute net force in 1D systems and prove that zero net force produces zero acceleration in both static (rest) and dynamic (constant speed) states.
activity: Dual Spring-Scale Tug-of-War: Teams use opposing calibrated spring scales attached to dynamics carts to establish balanced force states (F_left = F_right). Students verify that when net force is zero, carts remain at rest OR roll with constant velocity when pushed.
essentialQuestion: Why does an aircraft cruising at 500 mph at constant altitude experience exactly zero net force?

wicor.Writing: Writing mathematical summation proofs: ΣF = F_forward - F_friction = 0.
wicor.Inquiry: Investigating why engine thrust must match aerodynamic drag during steady cruising.
wicor.Collaboration: Coordinating spring scale pulls to maintain equilibrium during cart motion.
wicor.Organization: Structuring two-column proofs resolving vertical and horizontal force components.
wicor.Reading: Reading dual gauge readouts and calculating algebraic vector sums.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: A car cruises down the highway in a straight line at a steady speed of 65 mph. Is the net force acting on the car forward, backward, or zero?
bellRinger.explanation: The net force is zero! Because the car travels at constant velocity, its acceleration is zero (a = 0), which means all forward and resistive forces are balanced.

title: Unbalanced Forces Produce Acceleration
topic: Introducing Newton's Second Law: Cause and Effect
summary: Establish that an unbalanced net force (F_net ≠ 0) causes acceleration in the direction of the net force, introducing the proportionalities of Newton's 2nd Law.
activity: Fan-Cart Demonstration & Proportional Reasoning Sprint: Students observe a low-friction cart with an electric fan motor. When the fan is turned on, the cart speeds up continuously. Students predict what happens when net force doubles or cart mass doubles.
essentialQuestion: What determines whether a force makes an object speed up, slow down, or simply maintain its motion?

wicor.Writing: Documenting cause-and-effect relationships: F_net causes acceleration, mass resists it.
wicor.Inquiry: Testing conceptual ranking scenarios: ordering systems by magnitude of acceleration.
wicor.Collaboration: Table teams debating whether a heavy truck or light car accelerates faster under identical thrust.
wicor.Organization: Developing a concept map linking Unbalanced Force → Acceleration → Changing Velocity.
wicor.Reading: Reading and annotating historical explanations of Newton's Second Law.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: You push a box to the right with 30 N of force, while friction resists to the left with 10 N. What is the net force acting on the box, and what will happen to its motion?
bellRinger.explanation: The net force is 30 N - 10 N = 20 N to the right. Because there is an unbalanced net force, the box will accelerate to the right.

title: Newton's Second Law Lab — Part 1: Force vs. Acceleration
topic: Empirical Verification of a ∝ F_net (Constant Mass System)
summary: Empirically verify that acceleration is directly proportional to applied net force when system mass is held constant.
activity: Modified Atwood Track Lab: Students pull a constant-mass dynamics cart across a track using hanging masses (0.1 N, 0.2 N, 0.3 N, 0.4 N) suspended over an end pulley. Students measure acceleration with photogates or motion sensors, plot acceleration vs net force, and observe a linear trendline.
essentialQuestion: How does experimental data verify the direct proportionality between applied net force and acceleration?

wicor.Writing: Drafting lab analysis explaining how linear graph slope confirms direct proportionality.
wicor.Inquiry: Isolating variables by ensuring total system mass remains constant during force transfers.
wicor.Collaboration: Assigning lab station roles: mass handler, sensor operator, and data recorder.
wicor.Organization: Constructing clean data tables correlating applied force (N) with measured acceleration (m/s²).
wicor.Reading: Reading digital sensor readouts and interpreting linear regression plots.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: If you double the net force pushing a shopping cart while keeping the total mass the same, what happens to the cart's acceleration?
bellRinger.explanation: The acceleration doubles, because acceleration is directly proportional to net force (a ∝ F_net).

title: Newton's Second Law Lab — Part 2: Mass vs. Acceleration
topic: Empirical Verification of a ∝ 1/m & Derivation of F_net = m · a
summary: Empirically verify that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass under constant force, synthesizing the master equation F_net = m · a.
activity: Part 2 of Second Law Inquiry: Students maintain a constant hanging pulling force while systematically adding mass bars to the cart (0.5 kg, 1.0 kg, 1.5 kg). Students plot acceleration vs mass (inverse curve) and acceleration vs 1/mass (straight line), deriving the equation F_net = m · a.
essentialQuestion: Why is the relationship between mass and acceleration inverse rather than direct?

wicor.Writing: Writing a formal derivation of the equation F_net = m · a based on experimental slope values.
wicor.Inquiry: Transforming non-linear inverse curves into linear plots using inverse mass (1/m).
wicor.Collaboration: Comparing data across lab groups to confirm that the slope matches the constant pulling force.
wicor.Organization: Linearizing data tables with calculated 1/m columns.
wicor.Reading: Reading and comparing multiple graph representations of physical relationships.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: A 10 N net force pushes a 2 kg cart. What is the acceleration? If the mass is increased to 4 kg under the same force, what is the new acceleration?
bellRinger.explanation: For 2 kg: a = F / m = 10 N / 2 kg = 5.0 m/s². For 4 kg: a = 10 N / 4 kg = 2.5 m/s² (doubling mass cuts acceleration in half).

title: The Reality of Friction: Static vs. Kinetic
topic: Friction Forces (F_f = μ · F_N), Surface Interfaces, and Energy Dissipation
summary: Investigate why real-world objects slow down: surface microscopic interactions, static friction threshold vs kinetic sliding friction, and normal force dependence.
activity: Friction Block Pull Lab: Students drag weighted wooden blocks across sandpaper, vinyl, and cardboard using spring scales. They record the peak static 'breakaway' force versus the lower steady dragging kinetic force, and calculate the friction coefficient (μ = F_f / F_N).
essentialQuestion: Why does it always require more force to start an object sliding than to keep it sliding?

wicor.Writing: Describing the microscopic interactions (asperities/welds) that create friction forces.
wicor.Inquiry: Testing whether contact surface area changes sliding friction when mass is held constant.
wicor.Collaboration: Partner trials testing multiple surface materials and logging peak vs sliding forces.
wicor.Organization: Organizing data tables comparing static coefficient (μ_s) to kinetic coefficient (μ_k).
wicor.Reading: Interpreting spring force dial peaks during initial breakaway movement.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: Why is it noticeably harder to get a heavy stalled car moving from rest than it is to keep it rolling once it starts moving?
bellRinger.explanation: Static friction (which must be overcome to start moving) is higher than kinetic friction (which resists rolling/sliding motion once moving).

title: Multi-Force Problem Solving Workshop
topic: Calculating Net Force, Friction, and Resulting Acceleration
summary: Synthesize dynamics and kinematics: Given applied forces and friction, calculate F_net, determine a = F_net / m, and predict stopping distances or final speeds.
activity: Collaborative Whiteboard Problem-Solving Sprint: Student teams solve real-world automotive braking scenarios. Given vehicle mass, tire friction on dry vs icy pavement, and initial speed, teams calculate stopping acceleration and minimum braking distance.
essentialQuestion: How do engineers link tire friction coefficients directly to highway braking distance requirements?

wicor.Writing: Writing complete multi-step algebraic solution sequences with units at every step.
wicor.Inquiry: Analyzing how doubling initial speed quadruples the stopping distance required by brakes.
wicor.Collaboration: Team whiteboard problem solving where members take turns acting as solver, checker, and scribe.
wicor.Organization: Executing a structured 4-step problem solver: FBD → Net Force equation → a = F_net / m → Kinematics.
wicor.Reading: Extracting numerical parameters and hidden physical conditions (e.g. 'stops' means v_final = 0) from text.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: A 1,000 kg car accelerates forward with 3,000 N of engine thrust while encountering 1,000 N of air resistance and friction. What is the car's acceleration?

title: Newton's Third Law of Motion (Action-Reaction Pairs)
topic: Interaction Pairs: Equal Magnitude, Opposite Direction, Different Objects
summary: Explore Newton's Third Law: Forces always exist in pairs. When Object A exerts a force on Object B, Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on Object A.
activity: Dual Force Sensor Collisions & Skateboard Push-Offs: Students connect digital force sensors back-to-back and collide them, observing identical peak force spikes in opposite directions. Students test skateboard/rolling chair push-offs to observe mutual recoil.
essentialQuestion: When a mosquito hits a car windshield, which object experiences the greater force?

wicor.Writing: Writing paired force statements: 'Object A exerts a force on Object B; Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on Object A.'
wicor.Inquiry: Analyzing why equal forces produce vastly different accelerations when objects have different masses.
wicor.Collaboration: Conducting pair skateboard and force sensor recoil trials safely.
wicor.Organization: Creating an interaction-pair diagram clearly identifying the two interacting objects.
wicor.Reading: Reading and critiquing common misconceptions about action-reaction pairs.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: When a heavy football linebacker tackles a light running back, does the linebacker exert more force on the running back, or do they exert equal force on each other?
bellRinger.explanation: According to Newton's Third Law, they exert the exact same magnitude of force on each other! The lighter player experiences a greater acceleration due to smaller mass (a = F / m).

title: Resolving the Third Law Paradox & System Boundaries
topic: The Horse-and-Cart Dilemma: Why Motion Occurs Despite Equal Forces
summary: Tackle the classic conceptual paradox: 'If action and reaction forces are always equal and opposite, why doesn't everything cancel out?' (They act on different objects!).
activity: System Boundary Diagramming Sprint: Students draw boundary boxes around individual objects (the horse, the cart, the road). They discover that within the cart's system boundary, only the forward pull of the horse exists, which is not cancelled by the cart's backward pull on the horse.
essentialQuestion: Why can't action-reaction force pairs ever cancel each other out to prevent motion?

wicor.Writing: Composing a formal scientific rebuttal resolving the horse-and-cart paradox.
wicor.Inquiry: Investigating how external friction between horse hooves and the ground drives forward movement.
wicor.Collaboration: Structured Socratic debate: arguing from the horse's perspective vs the physics perspective.
wicor.Organization: Drawing dotted system boundary lines to isolate internal from external forces.
wicor.Reading: Analyzing historical philosophical debates on Newtonian action-reaction mechanics.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: When you walk across the floor, what physical object actually exerts the forward force that pushes your body forward?
bellRinger.explanation: The floor! Your foot pushes backward on the ground; by Newton's Third Law, the ground simultaneously pushes forward on your foot.

title: Crash Engineering & Safety: Forces in Collisions
topic: Impulse, Impact Time & Vehicle Safety Engineering
summary: Apply Newtonian mechanics to engineering safety: investigate how crumple zones, airbags, and seatbelts minimize lethal forces by extending impact duration.
activity: Collision Telemetry & Egg-Crash Cart Analysis: Students preview the Operation Safe Heeler crash engineering challenge. Students analyze high-speed video telemetry comparing rigid carts vs carts fitted with paper/foam crumple zones, calculating the dramatic drop in peak impact force.
essentialQuestion: How do automotive engineers manipulate contact time to minimize lethal forces during sudden deceleration?

wicor.Writing: Writing an engineering justification report evaluating crumple zone materials.
wicor.Inquiry: Analyzing accelerometer collision curves to compare peak force vs duration of impact.
wicor.Collaboration: Teams evaluating crumple zone prototypes under safety constraints.
wicor.Organization: Graphing force vs time curves and calculating the impulse area.
wicor.Reading: Reading national highway safety crash test standards and helmet design criteria.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: Why do cars have crumple zones designed to crush during a front-end collision instead of being built out of unbreakable, solid steel?
bellRinger.explanation: Crumpling extends the duration of the crash (increases Δt). Because impact force equals F = m · Δv / Δt, extending the stopping time dramatically lowers the force experienced by passengers.

title: Unit 2 Comprehensive Synthesis & Gallery Walk
topic: Master Review of Kinematics and Dynamics
summary: Unify the entire 5-week journey: from measuring distance and time to predicting acceleration and forces across multi-agent physical systems.
activity: Collaborative Problem Poster Gallery Walk: Teams create large-format solution posters for complex real-world challenges (rocket liftoff with decreasing mass, skydiving terminal velocity, multi-vehicle highway braking). Teams rotate with peer critique rubrics.
essentialQuestion: How do kinematic motion models and Newtonian force laws unite into a single predictive framework for all physical motion?

wicor.Writing: Constructing written peer critiques evaluating mathematical accuracy and graph annotations.
wicor.Inquiry: Synthesizing multi-week concepts into comprehensive multi-stage physical proofs.
wicor.Collaboration: Team poster construction and gallery walk peer review circles.
wicor.Organization: Formatting solution posters into quadrants: Given parameters, FBD, Motion Graphs, and Proof.
wicor.Reading: Reading peer posters and decoding alternative algebraic problem-solving strategies.

bellRinger.promptQuestion: Summarize Newton's Three Laws of Motion in one sentence each.
bellRinger.explanation: 1st Law: Objects keep their velocity unless acted on by a net force. 2nd Law: Unbalanced net force causes acceleration (F_net = m · a). 3rd Law: Every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force.

title: Unit 2 Summative Assessment
topic: Comprehensive Exam on 1D Kinematics & Newton's Laws of Motion
